case_analysis.focal_point: Whether lower federal courts may entertain (and potentially invalidate) FECA’s limits on coordinated political party expenditures in light of the Supreme Court’s decision in Colorado II rejecting a facial First Amendment challenge to the same limits.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) provisions limiting coordinated expenditures by political party committees with federal candidates (coordinated party expenditure limits), as challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs/petitioners argue that FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits unconstitutionally burden political speech and associational rights, and that Colorado II should not control because subsequent doctrinal developments in campaign-finance and First Amendment law (and additional arguments and factual/analytic distinctions they now present) have undermined Colorado II’s reasoning; they attempt to proceed at least as an as-applied challenge (and/or a renewed facial challenge) seeking a pathway for the Supreme Court to reconsider or overrule Colorado II.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC/respondent contends that Colorado II squarely forecloses the challenge because it upheld the constitutionality of coordinated party expenditure limits against materially the same First Amendment theory (treating coordinated spending as regulable to prevent circumvention of contribution limits); under vertical stare decisis (Rodriguez de Quijas), inferior courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent unless and until the Supreme Court itself overrules it, and plaintiffs cannot repackage the same arguments as an as-applied challenge to evade that binding holding.

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point remains that later decisions have narrowed the permissible anticorruption interest to quid pro quo corruption, arguably weakening Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale; but that is an argument for this Court to reconsider Colorado II, not for a lower court to treat it as displaced. Justice Kavanaugh correctly anchors the analysis in Rodriguez de Quijas: inferior courts must follow a directly controlling holding even if subsequent cases cast doubt on its reasoning, and Colorado II upheld these coordinated party-expenditure limits on the contribution-analogue theory that governs here. Justice Kagan is also right that an “as-applied” label cannot do the necessary work absent a materially distinct application or record that takes the case outside Colorado II’s holding. Given the institutional and administrability costs in election law, we should decide narrowly on vertical stare decisis and leave any reconsideration of Colorado II’s merits to a proper vehicle in this Court.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point—that later campaign-finance cases have narrowed the permissible governmental interest to quid pro quo corruption and thereby weakened Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale—at most supplies an argument for this Court to reconsider Colorado II, not for lower courts to disregard it. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Rodriguez de Quijas squarely forbids anticipatory overruling by inferior courts when a Supreme Court holding directly controls the same statutory provision and constitutional theory. Relabeling the challenge “as-applied” cannot evade Colorado II absent a materially distinct application that falls outside its contribution-analogue logic for coordinated party expenditures, and none is presented here. While I remain doubtful, on originalist grounds, about much of our modern campaign-finance doctrine, vertical stare decisis requires enforcing Colorado II until we expressly revisit it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest argument on the other side is that later cases narrowing permissible campaign-finance interests to quid pro quo corruption have “eroded” Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale, but Rodriguez de Quijas forecloses lower courts from treating erosion as authorization to disregard a directly controlling holding. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Colorado II upheld these very coordinated party-expenditure limits on the premise that coordination operates like a contribution and may be capped to protect the integrity of contribution limits; that holding squarely governs materially indistinguishable challenges. Relabeling the claim as “as-applied” cannot change the operative legal rule absent a genuinely distinct factual posture that avoids Colorado II’s contribution-analogue logic, and none is apparent here. The practical consequence of allowing lower courts to anticipate overruling in this domain would be instability and uneven enforcement of federal election law—precisely what vertical stare decisis is designed to prevent.

As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts stress, Rodriguez de Quijas squarely forbids “anticipatory overruling” when a precedent directly controls the same statute and the same core First Amendment theory, and an “as-applied” label cannot do the work without a materially distinct application or record. case_analysis.focal_point: Whether lower federal courts may entertain (and certify for en banc review) a constitutional challenge to FECA’s limits on coordinated party expenditures when the Supreme Court has already rejected a materially identical facial First Amendment challenge in Colorado II, and whether intervening doctrinal developments permit treating Colorado II as effectively displaced.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) provisions limiting coordinated expenditures by political party committees in connection with federal candidates (the “coordinated party expenditure limits”), challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs (challengers) argue that FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits unconstitutionally burden political speech and association because coordinated party spending should be treated like protected political expression rather than regulable contributions. They contend Colorado II should not control because subsequent campaign-finance and First Amendment decisions have changed the governing framework (doctrinal displacement), and because they raise new arguments and/or a different posture (e.g., as-applied framing or refined factual/legal theories) that purportedly were not presented or resolved in Colorado II. They further maintain that, at minimum, their claim is non-frivolous and warrants certification to the court of appeals sitting en banc even if it conflicts with existing Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC argues the challenge is foreclosed by binding Supreme Court precedent—Colorado II—which specifically upheld limits on coordinated party expenditures on the theory that coordinated spending can function as a contribution-like mechanism enabling circumvention of contribution limits. Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts must follow Colorado II unless and until the Supreme Court overrules it; lower courts cannot reach the merits of a claim that is substantively the same as one already rejected by the Supreme Court. The FEC also disputes attempts to relabel the case as ‘as-applied’ if it relies on the same factual and legal premises previously considered, and it contends the district court should not make broad “legislative fact” findings because FECA’s certification scheme reserves legal issues to the en banc court of appeals.

Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Exp., Inc., inferior courts may not treat a Supreme Court decision as implicitly overruled based on perceived “doctrinal displacement”; that judgment is reserved to this Court, and certification procedures cannot be used to evade vertical stare decisis. While Kennedy v. Bremerton notes that obviously abandoned reasoning should not be mechanically extended, it does not authorize lower courts to disregard a directly controlling merits holding like Colorado II in the campaign-finance context. Respecting procedural fairness and institutional regularity, the proper course is to apply Colorado II and leave any reconsideration of FECA’s coordinated party limits to the Supreme Court or Congress.
